paragraphs: In ancient India a great king was once asked four questions. One of them was this: what is the most wonderful thing in the world? The answer given was simply 'Hope.'

It really is astonishing, said Swamiji. Day and night we watch people around us die, and yet each of us quietly assumes we will not. We never imagine that we too will die, or that we too will suffer. Everyone believes success will come to them, against all the odds and against all logic.

Yet nobody here is ever completely happy. The man who is rich with plenty to eat has a stomach that won't let him enjoy it. The man who could digest anything has nothing to eat. One rich man has no children; one poor, hungry man has a crowd of children and no idea how to feed them.

Why does it work like this? Because happiness and misery are two sides of the same coin, Swamiji explained. Whoever picks up one has to take the other too. We cling to the foolish hope that we can have happiness without any misery, and that hope has gripped us so tightly that we have lost control over our senses.
learn: Hope keeps us going, but blind hope can stop us seeing life clearly. Expecting only the good side of the coin sets us up for disappointment. Learning to accept both sides calmly is a real kind of strength.
